sources.entry: JavaScript: _WTF is JSX (Let's Build a JSX Renderer)_

summary.title: WTF is JSX
summary.one_liner: JSX compiles to plain h() function calls that build a virtual DOM tree, and you can write a small renderer that turns that tree into real DOM nodes.
takeaways: JSX is transpiled into h() function calls; Babel supports this out of the box via the /** @jsx h */ pragma.
The h() function returns a simple object with nodeName, attributes and children, forming a virtual DOM tree.
A short render() function converts that virtual DOM into real DOM elements and text nodes using createElement, setAttribute and appendChild.
JSX lets you use plain JavaScript for iteration and logic (map, forEach, loops) instead of learning template-specific syntax, and avoids eval or code generation.
summary.summary: The article explains that JSX is syntactic sugar that Babel transpiles into calls to a function (conventionally h), declared through a per-file pragma comment. It walks through a before-and-after example and writes a minimal h() that builds nested objects, followed by a render() function that creates DOM nodes from them. The author then compares JSX with template languages, arguing that plain JavaScript for iteration and logic is preferable to limited template constructs or code generation. It closes with a full example that renders a list and shows the virtual DOM as JSON.
